tier_reason: The only numbers are in the README of the Rcsv Ruby wrapper (bench.rb is public: Ruby stdlib CSV.parse vs Rcsv.parse on test/test_rcsv.csv, 10 iterations, Benchmark.bmbm), but Ruby version, compiler, flags and CPU are all unstated, and it is not a peer-reviewed paper or a known independent suite, so C.

corrections.baseline: Ruby's stdlib CSV parser (bench.rb does require 'csv' and labels it FasterCSV, which became Ruby's stdlib csv in 1.9); a pure-Ruby parser, not a C or C++ incumbent
corrections.workload: Downstream benchmark in the Rcsv Ruby C extension (which embeds unmodified libcsv 3.0.3): bench.rb parses test/test_rcsv.csv (889 lines, about 167 KB, mixed quoted fields) 10 times with Rcsv.parse(data) in default mode (all fields returned as strings, no per-column conversion) versus CSV.parse(data), timed with Ruby Benchmark.bmbm; not libcsv's own benchmark and not a pure C comparison.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Rcsv (libcsv backend) 0.060 s user / 0.062248 s real versus FasterCSV (Ruby stdlib CSV) 0.580 s user / 0.618837 s real for 10 parses of the 167 KB test file, about 9.9x on real time and 9.7x on user time (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: libcsv's own README, man page and repo carry no benchmark; the only numbers are in the README of Rcsv (third-party Ruby wrapper, upstream arp/rcsv, of which 284km/rcsv is a 3-star fork with an identical README) against Ruby's pure-Ruby stdlib CSV parser from the Ruby 1.8/1.9 era (Rcsv was tested on REE, 1.8.7 to 2.2.2). Input is small (167 KB parsed 10 times) and Ruby version, hardware, compiler and flags are unstated; Ruby's csv gem has since been rewritten and is faster, so the ratio is stale and says nothing about libcsv against other C or C++ CSV parsers. The benchmark times object allocation of Ruby strings as well as parsing. Last commit 2021-08-20 (over 3 years ago), so abandoned, though the library is stable (version 3.0.3) and widely packaged as libcsv3. LGPL-2.1-or-later: dynamic linking or relinkable distribution obligations apply. No C or C++ shootout including libcsv was found.

notes: Numbers verified verbatim in the Rcsv README and bench.rb; benchmark_url moved from the 284km fork to upstream arp/rcsv (libcsv's README links fiksu/rcsv, now arp/rcsv). The record's caveat that Rcsv does per-column type conversion in this benchmark was wrong: bench.rb calls Rcsv.parse(data) with defaults. Keep at C with the shortcoming that the only evidence is a stale Ruby-wrapper comparison against a pure-Ruby parser, not against any C/C++ baseline.

tier_reason: First-party doc/Benchmarks.md with public code (test/benchmark.cc), -O3 and CPU (i7-8565U) stated, but no compiler name or version (only 'Debian10 libstdc++ package'), so not A; numbers are first-party, so C. The numbers show parity or a slowdown, not a win.

corrections.workload: test/benchmark.cc: 500,000 uint32_t keys from test/array.s3 (also wrapped in 69-byte and 444-byte structs) inserted then erased in set and map, and push_back then pop_back in list (and stack), each pass repeated 10 times; RDTSC ticks summed and divided by 500,000 x 10, so the table is average ticks per operation. The std::set/std::map baseline does find() then a hinted insert/erase to mimic cdada's E_EXISTS/E_NOT_FOUND semantics. Thread runs under SCHED_FIFO max priority. Measures libcdada's wrapper overhead over libstdc++.
corrections.claimed_speedup: No speedup claimed. README: 'Reasonable performance - comparable to libstdc++'. Table (average ticks per op, std vs cdada): uint32 set insert 752 vs 746, erase 698 vs 743; uint32 map insert 830 vs 809, erase 722 vs 1009; uint32 list push_back 20 vs 28, pop_back 17 vs 20; 69-byte set insert 1410 vs 1623 (custom container 1433); 69-byte list push_back 42 vs 67 (custom 44), pop_back 22 vs 40 (custom 25); 444-byte custom containers within about 4 percent except map erase 1472 vs 2021.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: -O3 (libcdada configured with ../configure, per doc); compiler name and version not stated, only 'Standard Debian10 libstdc++ package'; benchmark source test/benchmark.cc
corrections.caveats: Not a faster-than-std result: the doc is an overhead measurement of a C wrapper built on libstdc++ itself, and cdada is level with libstdc++ only on uint32 set/map inserts (within about 3 percent, in the noise) and on custom containers for large structs. It is slower on most other rows: uint32 map erase about 1.4x slower, list push_back about 1.4x slower, 69-byte list pop_back about 1.8x slower, 444-byte map erase about 1.37x slower (derived from page data). One 'random execution' of the binary, no variance given; compiler version missing; Debian 10 era libstdc++ only (no libc++ or MSVC STL). The 'list' rows time push_back/pop_back, not insert/erase. README calls map a hashmap, but it is backed by std::map. Not thread-safe. Kept for the C-callable container wrapper role.

notes: All table numbers verified on doc/Benchmarks.md; benchmark.cc shows ticks are per-operation averages over 10 runs (the record's 'tick normalisation not stated' was wrong) and that list rows are push_back/pop_back. Metadata confirmed: BSD-2-Clause, 30 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-03-01 (active). Shortcoming to record: not faster than libstdc++ (it wraps it), slower on erase and list rows; category sequence-containers fits only the list part (set/map are associative).
